title: Public-key encryption explained with paint
description: How can two strangers agree a secret while everyone watches? The classic paint-mixing analogy for public-key key exchange, and how HTTPS uses it.

scenes.big: How strangers share a secret in public
scenes.say: How can two strangers agree on a secret while everyone is listening? With paint.
You both agree on a public colour, say yellow. Each of you also picks a private colour, and never shares it.

steps: Mix your private colour into yellow
Swap the mixtures in the open
Both end with the same shade
scenes.say: Mix your private colour into the yellow, then swap mixtures in the open. Now add your private colour once more. You both end up with the exact same shade, but a spy can't unmix paint to find it.
That's the Diffie-Hellman idea. Computers do it with maths instead of paint. Your browser does it whenever you connect over HTTPS, then uses the shared secret as a fast key for the rest of the chat.
The secret itself never travels. Only the mixes do, and reversing them is the hard part. Follow for more security, minus the jargon.
